questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: What pre-Columbian written records establish
questions.learningObjective: say what a written record of dates and events proves about its makers
questions.stem: Before the arrival of Europeans, Maya communities kept painted manuscripts and carved stone inscriptions recording dated events. What do such records establish?

options.text: A tradition of keeping written accounts of events, carried out by trained specialists
A press for printing on paper, which the stone carvings show was in common use
options.misconception: confuses carved stone records with a printing technology they do not imply

options.text: The earliest surviving novels written in Europe before the year 1500
options.misconception: moves records made in Mesoamerica across the Atlantic and into a European literature

options.text: A currency of stamped metal, since carved dates would be needed to authorise payments
options.misconception: infers a minting practice from inscriptions that record events

questions.explanation: What a written record proves is literacy, and literacy is a practice with people behind it: someone had to be trained to read the signs and someone else to cut or paint them. Dated inscriptions that tie a named ruler to an event are evidence of an accounting practice, which is a specialist craft of the kind that states also need. That is the whole of the claim, and it is broad enough to be certain of: writing for monumental record and for books on bark paper both existed in the Maya world well before 1500. Nothing in this evidence reaches a press, since carving stone and painting bark are hand processes, and a novel is a literary form these documents are not. A stamped coin would be evidence of a different technology altogether, and the argument that links the two is a link the record itself never makes.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of work the existence of dated written records implies.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Reading two sets of records against each other
questions.learningObjective: read a contrast between two bodies of evidence and limit the claim
questions.stem: After the conquest of Tenochtitlan, later European accounts give a far lower figure for the population than the records kept locally. What does that contrast let a historian claim?

options.text: That a large population loss is well attested, while the share owed to disease remains argued
That the local records are unreliable and should be set aside in favour of the later ones
options.misconception: throws out one whole body of evidence because it disagrees with another

options.text: That no such loss occurred and that the later European figures were invented
options.misconception: reads a disagreement between sources as proof that the event itself did not happen

options.text: That the loss can be stated to a single figure, since two independent sets of numbers exist
options.misconception: believes two disagreeing sources average out into one accurate quantity

questions.explanation: Two sets of evidence that disagree strengthen the fact and weaken the detail. Historians generally take a serious population fall after the conquest of Tenochtitlan as well attested, and they also accept that the surviving estimates vary widely, so a claim that there was a catastrophe is safer than a claim about its size. The two kinds of record were made for different purposes and with different tools, which is why they differ, and neither is disqualified by the disagreement. The causes are the part that stays open, since epidemic disease, warfare and the flight of people all appear in the accounts and cannot be separated cleanly in most estimates. A historian who declared the local records worthless would be discarding the evidence that makes the fall visible at all, and one who announced a single figure would be claiming a precision the sources do not supply.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the story two disagreeing sources can settle and which part they cannot.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Officials named in colonial records
questions.learningObjective: group colonial office titles by the authority they carried
questions.stem: Sixteenth-century Spanish records mention a gobernador, a corregidor and un adelantado. What does that set of titles name?

options.text: Officials sent out from the centre to hold authority in particular districts
Local nobles given titles by the crown so that they would raise troops for it
options.misconception: reads appointed officials of the crown as hereditary nobles with military duties

options.text: Merchants granted a monopoly over trade in return for funding the colony
options.misconception: confuses administrative office with a commercial grant from the same crown

options.text: Clergy put in charge of the doctrine taught to the population
options.misconception: takes titles of government office for titles of ecclesiastical office

questions.explanation: The grouping is by function, and the three titles in this set all belong to government: a corregidor administered justice and order in a district, an adelantado held authority on a frontier, and a gobernador governed a larger unit. What they share is the source of the office, since each was appointed from the centre and answerable upwards, which is what distinguishes a colonial administration from the local authority that existed before it. The words matter in the sources because a document naming an office is naming a chain of responsibility, and a reader who cannot place the title cannot say who was being asked to do what. Titles of nobility belong to a different register and carry no duty to administer a district, a monopoly is granted to a person or a company rather than to a post, and ecclesiastical titles are given to clergy, so none of those readings fits a record of appointment.
questions.hint: Ask what these offices have in common in terms of who appointed them and to whom they answer.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: How a late colonial independence campaign worked
questions.learningObjective: identify the method of an independence movement from the evidence it left
questions.stem: A late colonial independence campaign left pamphlets arguing from natural rights, claims made by local juntas, and port records showing new foreign shipping. What method does that combine point to?

options.text: Argument in print, authority claimed locally, and outside trade used as leverage
A rejection of every idea that reached the colony from beyond its own borders
options.misconception: reads the use of natural-rights argument as a refusal of outside influence

options.text: A question settled by arms, with no argument put into print before the fighting began
options.misconception: assumes a campaign with printed pamphlets must have avoided military means

options.text: An attempt to keep the colonial government exactly as it had been before
options.misconception: confuses local claims of authority with a wish to preserve the old order untouched

questions.explanation: The evidence points to a campaign that worked on three fronts at once, and each kind of document shows a different one. Pamphlets printed in the last decades of the colonial period argue from the language of natural rights, which is a European inheritance used against colonial rule, so the second distractor has the direction of the borrowing backwards. A junta claiming to govern in the king's absence turns local administration into a political claim, and the port records show a colonial economy being used as a lever, since trade was what the metropole regulated. Independence campaigns of this period were therefore political arguments, administrative claims and economic pressure together, and the old government was not what they were asking to keep. Treating any one of the three as the whole of the method throws away the other two.
questions.hint: Ask what each kind of document shows the campaign doing, then add the three together.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: What an article of a constitution does
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a binding rule on the state from a statement of practice
questions.stem: A constitution's first article reads 'Toda persona tiene derecho a la igualdad y a no ser discriminada'. What kind of statement is that article making?

options.text: A rule that binds the state and stands above an ordinary law that contradicts it
A suggestion to the legislature, to be applied as that house finds convenient
options.misconception: reads a constitutional right as an optional piece of advice

options.text: A description of how the government is in fact organised at present
options.misconception: mistakes a rule that should hold for a report of what does hold

options.text: A request addressed to other countries for protection against discrimination
options.misconception: sends a statement of internal law out to foreign governments

questions.explanation: The grammar marks the force of the claim as much as the history does. Toda persona is a quantified noun phrase with no restriction, and the verb tiene derecho a is present indicative rather than a conditional, so the article asserts a right that exists now and does not depend on anyone's permission. Two prepositional phrases follow the same pattern, a la igualdad and a no ser discriminada, and the second is a negative purpose clause, which is how Spanish names a thing a person must not be made to suffer. A constitution is the highest law of a country precisely so that an ordinary law cannot quietly remove such a right, which is the sense in which it stands above. Advice, description and foreign request are three other kinds of statement, and the indicative form of the verb rules all three of them out.
questions.hint: Ask whether the verb asserts, suggests or describes, and how wide its subject is.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: The mechanism of an agrarian reform
questions.learningObjective: name the two steps of a land redistribution
questions.stem: An agrarian reform is described as taking unused estates into public ownership and granting the land to landless farm workers. Which mechanism does that describe?

options.text: Expropriation first, then redistribution to the people who work the ground
A reduction in tax for the owners of the largest estates in the region
options.misconception: reads a reform of landownership as a change in the tax treatment of owners

options.text: A loan scheme under which tenants buy the ground they have long rented
options.misconception: confuses a grant of land with a purchase made on credit

options.text: A change of frontier that moved several villages into a different province
options.misconception: takes a change in land tenure for a change in administrative borders

questions.explanation: The description names two steps in an order, and the order is the mechanism. Ownership is changed first, since land cannot be granted by people who hold no title to it, and only then is it regranted to those who farm it, which is what the word redistribuir requires. Such reforms were carried out in several countries of the region in the twentieth century, and the sequence expropriation and then settlement is the part of the account that is broadly agreed, whatever differs in the years and in the size of holdings. A tax reduction leaves ownership where it is and merely changes the income of the owner, and a loan scheme puts land on the market instead of taking it off it. The trap of reading a tenure reform as a frontier change is worth naming because both alter maps, which is why a map is a poor guide to what a reform did.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two steps has to come first, and what a title is needed for.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: The programme of a twentieth-century revolution
questions.learningObjective: sort the measures of a revolutionary government by the field they change
questions.stem: A revolution of the twentieth century is summarised as taking the railways into public ownership, expanding literacy programmes and giving the country a new written constitution. What kind of programme is that?

options.text: A state programme that changes ownership, schooling and institutions in the same period
A private scheme run by foreign companies for their own commercial benefit
options.misconception: reads a transfer to public ownership as a transfer to private hands

options.text: An alliance between two states against a third, fought without any change to the country
options.misconception: treats a domestic programme of reform as a foreign war

options.text: A revival of folk music that left property and schooling exactly as they were
options.misconception: confuses a programme of structural reform with a cultural movement

questions.explanation: The three measures belong to three different fields, and a revolutionary programme is recognisable by changing all of them at once. Ownership of a key industry is an economic decision, an expansion of literacy is a social one, and a new constitution is an institutional one, and a government that does all three has not made a gesture but has rebuilt how the country is run. Revolutions in Latin America in the twentieth century varied enormously in how far they got, and the exact list is different in each case, but the shape of the claim is what makes them recognisable as programmes rather than as episodes. A foreign war leaves the domestic order in place, and a cultural revival changes what people listen to rather than who owns the railways, which is why the first and fourth readings both lose the programme.
questions.hint: Ask which field each of the three measures belongs to, and what a government that changes all three is doing.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: The mechanism of an authoritarian period
questions.learningObjective: recognise control that reaches the parties, the press and the workplace together
questions.stem: An authoritarian period is described as banning opposition parties, censoring the press and punishing employers who hire the dismissed. What kind of control does that describe?

options.text: Control reaching the parties, the media and the workplace at the same time
Control of the armed forces alone, with the rest of the state left untouched
options.misconception: picks out the one institution not named in the description

options.text: Control through elections held more often than in a democracy
options.misconception: supposes that a ban on parties and the press would be paired with more elections

options.text: Control through taxation, with the media and the parties left free
options.misconception: substitutes a fiscal instrument for the three named instruments

questions.explanation: The three measures are chosen because they close the three places where opposition could organise. Ban the parties and there is no body that can state a collective claim; censor the press and no claim reaches the population; then the last one closes the loophole that survived, since people who cannot organise can still find one another at work, and an employer who takes on the dismissed is punished. What makes the mechanism recognisable is that it operates through ordinary institutions rather than by cancelling them, and the description is of exactly that kind. Banning parties and the press while holding more elections is a combination no historian has recorded, because the two measures cancel each other, and taxation has no bearing on what anyone is allowed to publish. The interesting part for a reader is the third measure, since it is the one that reaches into daily life.
questions.hint: Ask what each of the three measures removes, and whether they cover the same ground.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: What a democratic transition puts in place
questions.learningObjective: identify the institutions that decide outcomes after military rule ends
questions.stem: A return to civilian government is described as restoring an elected assembly, an independent court and a free press. What does that description identify?

options.text: The bodies that settle who governs, who judges and what is published
The ministries that existed under the previous government and survived the change
options.misconception: reads a new settlement of authority as continuity of the old one

options.text: The economic measures used to lower prices in the first year of the change
options.misconception: confuses institutions of the state with measures of economic policy

options.text: The local councils that were abolished and replaced by appointed mayors
options.misconception: assumes a democratic transition removes local government rather than opening it

questions.explanation: Each of the three names answers a different question, and together they cover the ways a modern state can be held to account. An elected assembly settles who governs, an independent court settles what the law means when it is tested, and a free press lets the reasons be argued in public rather than settled in private. A transition is precisely the transfer of those three decisions away from whoever had been making them without reference to anyone else, so the description is of institutions and not of personalities. Ministers can survive a change without any of this happening, since a ministry is a department of an administration rather than a limit on it, and economic measures belong to a different chapter altogether. Local government is usually part of what a transition opens up, so the fourth reading has the direction of the change reversed.
questions.hint: Ask which question each of the three bodies answers, and who decides it.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Why a migration wave began when it did
questions.learningObjective: tell a push factor from a pull factor using dated evidence
questions.stem: Two waves of emigration from one country are dated, the first to a failed harvest and the second to a run of factory closures. Which factors does that dating identify?

options.text: Push factors, since both waves follow a worsening of conditions at home
Pull factors, since the deciding argument was the better wage waiting abroad
options.misconception: reads conditions at home as arguments made by the country being entered

options.text: Legal factors, since both dates mark a change in the border regulations
options.misconception: takes a coincidence in timing to mean the law changed on those dates

options.text: Family factors, since every migrant in both waves travelled with relatives
options.misconception: assumes a uniform motive inside a whole migration wave

questions.explanation: A push factor is a pressure that makes leaving necessary or sensible, and the two events named are both of that kind: a harvest that failed removes the work, and a run of closures removes the wage. The test is where the pressure is felt, and in both waves it was felt in the country being left, which is what fixes the direction. Pull factors are the attractions of the destination, and they were present across long periods in which nobody left, so they cannot explain a change in the rate. The dating is doing real work here, since a coincidence with a harvest failure is evidence and a coincidence with a change of statute is an assumption unless the records say so, and family networks do account for much of who travelled but not for the timing of the wave. Historians usually say both kinds of factor operate together, which is why the item is worth reading as a distinction rather than a choice.
questions.hint: Ask where the pressure in each event was felt, and what the pull argument would need to explain.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: What a remittance figure does and does not show
questions.learningObjective: limit a claim about money sent to households
questions.stem: A report says that money sent home by people abroad pays for a large share of household spending in one region, measured against local wages. What has that statement shown?

options.text: That a measurable flow reaches households and is large beside the wages available there
That the flow has replaced most of what the region produces, since wages matter no longer
options.misconception: turns a large share of household spending into a share of national production

options.text: That the flow depends wholly on the entry rules of one foreign country
options.misconception: supposes a flow from many countries to turn on one country's rules alone

options.text: That the amount has been counted exactly, by a single official and reconciled series
options.misconception: reads a measured comparison as an exact count from a single source

questions.explanation: The statement is carefully limited and the item is about where the limit lies. Money that arrives from abroad can be compared with the wages earned locally, and in several countries of the region that share is large enough to matter to household spending, which is a broad and well-attested finding. What the statement does not do is reach production: a transfer is income received, and income received is not the same thing as what a place makes, so a large share of spending can sit alongside an economy whose output has not moved. Nor does it reduce to one country's rules, since the flow in most cases comes from several destinations at once, and any figure compiled from records will carry the gap between what is declared and what is not. The fourth trap is the one to name: a comparison against wages is a measurement, not a census of every peso sent.
questions.hint: Ask what a transfer received is, and what it would have to be to count as output.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Which sectors a trade agreement actually changes
questions.learningObjective: read an uneven trade agreement and name who gains
questions.stem: A trade agreement is described as lowering tariffs on manufactured goods while leaving agricultural quotas in place. What does that description establish?

options.text: That the gains fall unevenly across sectors, with industry favoured over agriculture
That every sector gains in the same proportion as the tariff that was cut
options.misconception: assumes a single cut produces a single proportional benefit everywhere

options.text: That the agreement removes every barrier between the parties, since barriers are its subject
options.misconception: reads one kind of measure as the whole content of an agreement

options.text: That agriculture was left out of the agreement, since its quotas are not mentioned
options.misconception: treats an unchanged measure as an excluded subject

questions.explanation: An agreement is read by asking which measure applies to which sector, and here the two measures do not match. Manufactured goods face a lower tariff, so imports from the partner become cheaper and producers there face more competition, while agricultural quotas stay as they were, so farmers are protected from exactly that. That asymmetry is the substance of the arrangement rather than a detail of it, and a reader who wants to know who the agreement favours should look for the measure that was left alone. An unchanged quota is not the same as an excluded subject, since agriculture is covered by the agreement and simply protected, which is why the fourth reading gets the words right and the meaning wrong. A cut to one line in one schedule cannot deliver a uniform benefit, and the presence of barriers in the text is the ordinary case rather than a contradiction of its purpose.
questions.hint: Ask which measure covers which sector, and what an unchanged measure implies.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Which group a fall in border crossings describes
questions.learningObjective: read a change in a statistic and identify the population it covers
questions.stem: A country's figures show a long-standing movement of people across its border falling sharply once a new permit system begins. Which group does that fall describe?

options.text: People who had been crossing without the documents the new system requires
The workers who had crossed with papers and had registered for employment
options.misconception: counts the documented flow, which the new system would not discourage

options.text: The merchants whose goods used to cross under the older customs rule
options.misconception: reads a movement of people as a movement of goods across a customs post

options.text: The students enrolled in courses offered outside the country
options.misconception: assumes enrolment abroad fell because a domestic permit system was introduced

questions.explanation: A new permit system raises the cost of crossing without the papers, and the flow that falls is the one that was already undocumented, so the fall measures that group rather than the whole. The direction of the figure is worth noticing: a measure that makes regularisation harder does not usually reduce the number of people already holding documents, and any such reduction would be a separate finding that the description does not report. The reasoning is by what the measure touches, which is the same test used for any policy statistic, and it is why a fall in crossings is normally read as evidence about the undocumented flow and not about migration in general. Customs traffic in goods and enrolment abroad belong to different systems with their own figures, and neither of them responds to a permit for people in the way described.
questions.hint: Ask which group the new measure makes more expensive, and which group it leaves untouched.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: What a language policy achieves and what it does not
questions.learningObjective: separate official standing from change in daily use
questions.stem: A policy gives an indigenous language official standing in a region and orders schools to teach in it, while census returns still show most speakers living in a few villages. What has the policy achieved?

options.text: Official standing for the language without a corresponding change in ordinary daily use
A settled position as the everyday language of towns and schools across the region
options.misconception: takes official standing in law for a settled position in daily life

options.text: A replacement of the dominant language in every public and private sphere at once
options.misconception: assumes a legal decision changes the speech of private households

options.text: The disappearance of the language, since a policy is meant to close it down
options.misconception: takes a language official in law to be a language abolished in practice

questions.explanation: Two things have happened and only one of them is what a policy can do directly. The language now has standing in law, which means a court, a school and an office must take it seriously, and that is a real gain. Daily use is a different matter, because a family decides what to speak at the table and a child acquires a language from the people closest to it, neither of which a decree reaches. The census figures in the description are the evidence for the gap, and the gap between legal standing and daily use is the standard finding wherever a minority language has been made official. The policy is therefore contested rather than either triumph or disaster, which is why a reader should be careful with the fourth reading: a policy that named a language made room for it, and no result on a census is a reason to describe that result as an aim.
questions.hint: Ask what a decree can change and what a household chooses for itself.

questions.topic: A literary claim about the language to be used
questions.learningObjective: state the claim a literary group made about vernacular usage
questions.stem: A group of writers in the late nineteenth century argued that a serious literature could be built from ordinary spoken Spanish, and edited a journal to show it. What claim were they making?

options.text: That everyday speech was fit to carry literature, rather than a defect to be corrected
That literature should be written in a language foreign to the people who read it
options.misconception: inverts the argument for the vernacular into an argument against it

options.text: That written usage had to be fixed by an authority before it could be used at all
options.misconception: reads a claim for the vernacular as a demand for more official regulation

options.text: That regional differences had to be removed before poetry was possible
options.misconception: turns an acceptance of regional speech into a demand for a single form

questions.explanation: The claim is about who owns the language. A group that edits a journal to publish in ordinary speech is making an argument that the elevated style then in fashion was a habit rather than a standard, and that the material of real conversation and regional usage can carry serious work. It is a claim about the fitness of a register, and it was argued in several countries of the Spanish-speaking world in the closing decades of the nineteenth century, in groups whose names and programmes differ but whose point about the vernacular is broadly the same. A demand for a foreign language, for a language fixed by an authority and for the removal of regional varieties are three different programmes, and the last of them is the opposite of what a writer working in regional speech would want. A journal is the right evidence to look at, since a claim about usage is best tested in a thing that was actually printed.
questions.hint: Ask what a journal printed in ordinary speech is designed to demonstrate.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Steps in dating an old document
questions.learningObjective: sequence the checks a historian makes to date a record
questions.stem: Five steps a historian takes to date an old document have been listed out of order. Which sequence is the working order?

options.text: Establish what kind of record it is, so the right evidence applies to it
Read the parts naming a maker, an office or an authority
Note any date written on it, on the face or in the seals
Compare its names, titles and offices with records of the same period
Test whether the claimed date fits the paper, the script and the references

questions.explanation: The order runs from the general to the particular, and each step depends on the one before it. Naming the kind of record comes first because it decides which evidence counts: a notarial instrument is dated by its notary and a printed broadsheet by its press, so the rest of the work cannot begin until the type is known. The maker and the office come next, since a document is dated by the authority that issued it, and only then is it worth reading a date written on the record, which may be a copy, a transcription or a later endorsement. Comparison with other records of the same kind is what turns a stated date into a corroborated one, and the material test comes at the end because it is the slowest and the one that can overturn the rest. A historian who started at the paper would be working without knowing what to look for.
questions.hint: Ask which step decides what kind of evidence is worth looking at, and which step can overturn the others.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: The institutions a regional agreement creates
questions.learningObjective: name the institutions of a supranational body and what each does
questions.stem: A regional agreement sets up a parliament, a council of governments, a court and a permanent secretariat. What has that arrangement created?

options.text: Its own institutions, so some decisions no longer depend on one capital alone
A single new capital that replaces the national government of each member
options.misconception: assumes shared institutions mean a single national government instead

options.text: A currency whose value is fixed by the permanent secretariat of the body
options.misconception: makes a permanent office into a monetary authority on that account

options.text: A private club whose members are the governments and whose rules bind nobody
options.misconception: treats an agreement between states as though it had no binding force

questions.explanation: The four names are the standard parts of a body created by treaty among states, and each one is a room in which a different kind of decision is made. A parliament is elected by the citizens of the members, a council brings the governments together, a court settles what the treaty means when the parties differ, and a secretariat is the permanent staff that keeps the work going between meetings. Together they mean that some questions leave the sole competence of each capital and are decided at the level of the group, which is the whole point of such an agreement. A new capital would replace member governments, which no treaty of this kind does; a currency is a separate question handled by a separate body; and a set of rules that binds nobody would be a discussion rather than an institution. The test is simple: ask who can take a binding decision and to whom that decision is addressed.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four bodies can make a decision that binds a member government.

options.misconception: describes a cut elsewhere when the sentence names money raised

options.misconception: reverses what borrowing does to a government's accounts

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: What an official's letter can and cannot prove
questions.learningObjective: explain why a document is evidence of a claim and not of the event
questions.stem: Explain why a letter written by a colonial official to his superior is solid evidence of what the official claimed, and not of what had happened, and say what makes such a letter useful all the same.

answer.exemplar: The document was written by somebody with a reason to make a particular case look right, and a letter up a hierarchy is where that reason is strongest. The official is reporting upwards, so the tone of the letter is a request for a decision, a justification already made, or a warning that lets him be seen to have raised it. Every one of those is a fact about him, and a fact about him is exactly what the letter is good evidence of. What it cannot do is report the thing itself, because nobody had yet been in a position to check it, and because the writer is the only source we have. That is why the letter is a primary source with a bias written into its structure rather than a description of events. The usefulness is not small. A letter shows what a colonial administration thought was going on, what it considered a problem worth a letter at all, and what language it used for people it was writing about, and those three things are evidence of the same order as any other record. Read in a series, with the replies and the later reports beside it, a letter becomes a way of following a policy from the moment it was proposed. The trap is to expect it to be a report, and a reader who keeps expecting one will either believe the writer or throw the letter away, and the better course is to ask what the writer needed the reader to think.

questions.hint: Ask what the writer needed the reader to think, and who had been in a position to check.

It is arranged and described in a record that can be searched
It is stored under conditions that slow the damage down
A reader asks for it and consults it under supervision

An archive that described before evaluating would spend the effort on items it was about to refuse.
questions.hint: Ask which step decides what is kept, and which one makes an item findable.

questions.learningObjective: distinguish a strong correlation from an identified cause
questions.stem: A physician records that cases of a fever fall sharply in one street after its water is drawn from a new source. What has been shown?

The organism that causes the fever, found and named at last
options.misconception: confuses a pattern in the cases with the identification of a cause

options.text: That every case in the district came from that one street
options.misconception: turns a fall in one place into a claim about every case everywhere

options.text: That the new supply of water is harmless, since the illness stopped with it
options.misconception: reads a fall in a disease as a verdict of safety on the water

questions.explanation: The observation is a comparison, and a comparison of this kind is powerful. questions.topic: What an astronomer's observation of motion reports
questions.learningObjective: interpret a measured motion against a fixed background
questions.stem: An astronomer reports a faint object in the sky that shifts position against the background stars over several months. What has been observed?

options.misconception: reads a motion against the stars as motion through the galaxy

options.text: A cloud of gas seen edge on, whose shape is revealed only by its movement
options.misconception: supplies an astronomical category the observation itself does not give

options.text: An instrument fault, since no such motion could occur in a fixed and distant sky
options.misconception: declares the observation impossible instead of asking what caused it

The second trap confuses motion relative to a distant field with motion inside the galaxy, and the third supplies a category that the report of a position does not contain. The fourth is worth naming as a habit: a careful observer always asks whether the apparatus is capable of the movement before believing the movement.
questions.hint: Ask what the background is doing, and what a small instrument fault would imitate.

options.text: That the subject must be identified exactly before any treatment of it begins
options.misconception: reads a claim about paint as a rule about the choice of subject

options.misconception: moves the origin to the place the form travelled to later

options.misconception: explains a form by the industry that later recorded it

options.text: An origin in a religious service, from which every later use was a departure
options.misconception: supplies a sacred origin for a form first played at celebrations

A genre's origin is a question about people and places, not about dates of publication.

questions.topic: Writing a museum label

questions.stem: Stage one: write a label in Spanish of no more than twenty words for an object in a public collection. Stage two: say what your label leaves out that a visitor would need in order to judge it.

That is the trade a label makes, and it makes it deliberately: a room holds a hundred objects and a visitor spends seconds in front of each, so the label has to be a label. The grammatical choices are carrying weight in the few words available. Siglo XIII is a date given in the shape museums use rather than a year, the prepositional phrase about the excavation attaches the object to an origin without spending a clause on it, and the two nouns in the last group say who holds it and how it came, which is the information a label is expected to give. A worse label would spend its words on praise. The habit worth teaching is to write the label, then ask which single fact a visitor could not do without.

questions.topic: Two accounts naming opposite causes of the same war
questions.learningObjective: read two opposing explanations and locate the difference between them
questions.stem: Official accounts of a war in the 1930s call it a defence against outside intervention, while the memoirs of those who fought call it a class struggle. What do the two accounts show?

options.text: That the cause named depends on which side is doing the naming, and both were written to persuade
That the war had two causes, each of which was in fact correct on its own
options.misconception: turns a disagreement between accounts into a settled list of causes

options.text: That the memoirs are of no value, since they were written by people who took part
options.misconception: discards a body of evidence on the ground of who wrote it

options.text: That the official account is a neutral summary and the memoirs are only an opinion
options.misconception: gives one source a neutrality that the form of the document does not supply

questions.explanation: Two accounts naming different causes is a normal condition of the record, and the interesting fact is that each is persuasive. An official account has to justify a position to the country and to the outside, so a war is framed as a defence, and a set of memoirs has to make sense of a campaign fought, so a class reading is available to the people who did the fighting. Neither is worthless for that reason, and the first trap is the commonest error in this kind of question, which is to decide that one side must be lying. A neutral summary would look different: it would name both explanations and the evidence for each, which neither document does.
questions.hint: Ask what each writer needed the reader to conclude, and why they needed it.

questions.topic: A novel used as evidence of its own moment
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a novel as a record of expectations from a record of events
questions.stem: A novelist published a long novel in 1925 about the wars of a continent, and a historian treats it as evidence of how that generation imagined the war. What is being claimed?

options.text: That the book is evidence of what readers expected in 1925, not a record of the war itself
That the book is an eyewitness account written by somebody who fought in the war
options.misconception: turns a published novel into the testimony of a participant

options.text: That the publication date settles the date of the events the book describes
options.misconception: moves from when a book appeared to when its subject happened

options.text: That every later reader has understood the war in the same way as the first
options.misconception: assumes one book's reception stands for the reading of a whole century

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A song as historical evidence
questions.learningObjective: explain what a song can prove and what has to be established first
questions.stem: Explain why a song with no public event in it can still be historical evidence, and say what a historian has to establish before drawing a conclusion from it.

answer.exemplar: A song is evidence of a mood before it is evidence of a fact, and moods are what the written record is worst at keeping. A government may not say in writing that a war has worn a country out, and a newspaper may not report what people sing in the kitchen, but a song repeats what the kitchen is saying, and it does so to an audience that chose to sing it. The song is also a document with a date and a route through space, since it travels with singers, on records and across a border, and the shape of that route can show which communities were talking to which and when. What has to be established first is the provenance: who sang it, where, for whom, and when, because a song performed at a festival in a later decade is a different document from the same tune sung by workers at the time. The second thing is the distinction between the words and the occasion, since a lyric may describe an older event while the tune is new, and historians who use a song have to be able to say which part of it belongs to the moment they are writing about. Neither half of the answer needs a lyric quoted in the history, and that is the practical point: the evidence is in the singing, in the date and in the place, all of which are outside the text.

questions.hint: Ask what a written record does not usually report, and what has to be known before a song is used.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Why a written date is weaker evidence than the object
questions.learningObjective: explain the difference between a stated date and a material one
questions.stem: Explain why a date written on a document is weaker evidence than the material of the document it is written on.

answer.exemplar: The two kinds of evidence fail in different ways, and that is the whole comparison. A written date is a statement, and statements can be wrong, copied, mistranscribed or copied from a model, and a person with a reason to be believed later has every opportunity to alter it, which is why a date in a hand that belongs to a copy is a date of the copy and nothing else. The material of a document is not a statement. Paper is made in one place and in periods, a seal can be compared with a matrix that is documented, and a script has habits that a forger can copy more easily than a forger can buy the right linen. The practical rule that follows is to use the material as the floor and the written date as the ceiling of a range, and to say so in the argument rather than picking the figure that is convenient. Neither is automatically right, and the interesting cases are the ones where they disagree, because a disagreement is itself evidence: a document that is genuinely old and states a much later year is a copy, a record, or a copy made for a purpose that has to be explained. The transferable habit is to ask what any particular piece of evidence can be wrong about before deciding how much weight it will carry.

questions.hint: Ask what a statement can be and what a physical object cannot easily be made to say.

options.misconception: infers a denial of any role from a promise of a role

questions.explanation: A clause of intention is a promise about the future written in the past, and the text is the only place where it exists. The treaty says the new administration will consult the inhabitants, which is a commitment the signatories accepted and a reader can quote, and that is a genuine and useful fact about the document. What the document cannot do is tell us what happened next, and the decades after a cession are a separate question requiring separate records, since consultation is exactly the kind of thing that is promised in a paragraph and omitted in a file. The second trap is the commonest error with this kind of clause, because the future of the sentence and the past of the narration sit in the same paragraph. The fourth trap is a reaction to a promise, not a reading of it, and a promise of a role is evidence that somebody intended a role to exist.
questions.hint: Ask whether the text reports a consultation or undertakes to arrange one.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Why two historians describe one period differently
questions.learningObjective: explain what an academic disagreement is made of
questions.stem: Explain why two historians can describe the same twenty years very differently, and say what their disagreement is actually made of.

answer.exemplar: Disagreement about a period is almost never disagreement about events, because events are what both of them accept. It is disagreement about which events are the ones that explain the rest, and that is a question of weight rather than of fact. One historian may treat a strike as a consequence of earlier wage cuts and another as the moment a movement discovered it could act, and both are describing the same twenty years with the same documents. A second source of difference is the choice of series, since a study built on wages will find a period of hardship and a study built on output will find a period of expansion, and neither is lying. A third is the vocabulary of explanation, where one side reaches for class and the other for institutions or for contingency, and a good answer will note that these words hide as much as they reveal. What the disagreement is made of, then, is not a list of facts but a set of priorities, and the useful habit is to read the two accounts as two arguments, ask what each of them explains well, and then decide which of the two questions is the one being asked. A historian who expects a settled version has set a standard that the discipline was not built to meet.

questions.hint: Ask whether the two accounts disagree about what happened or about what explains it.

questions.explanation: A good answer refuses the idea that disagreement is about events and locates it in weight instead, then gives two concrete sources of difference and one trap. The two sources are the choice of series, where a study built on wages and a study built on output describe the same period in opposite terms, and the vocabulary of explanation, where one side reaches for class and another for institutions or contingency. The trap is the argument that one of the two accounts has the facts and the other has opinions, which is a description of a first draft rather than of a piece of history. The transferable half is the reading habit, since a second account is only useful if it is read as a second argument with its own priorities, and the question worth asking of either is which of the two it explains better.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A map as a document with a date
questions.learningObjective: explain what a map is evidence of besides the territory it shows
questions.stem: Explain why a map drawn in one century is evidence about the century that drew it and not a picture of the territory it shows.

answer.exemplar: A map is a set of decisions about what to leave out, and the decisions are made by somebody at a particular moment with a particular purpose. A military office wants roads, heights and the range of a gun; a commercial house wants ports and distances; a school wants whatever fits a lesson. Each of them produces a map in which something a modern reader considers obvious is simply not there, and none of them is lying, because the map never claimed to be a photograph. What the object therefore shows first is the purpose it was made for, and that is why an old map is evidence about the century that drew it: the borders it draws are the borders somebody claimed, the blank spaces are the places the draughtsman was told to leave alone, and the paper and the lettering date the drawing independently of the territory. The strongest form of the answer uses a case where the omission is a decision, such as a settlement left off a map of a frontier precisely because it was a problem, and then notes that the omission is legible to a modern reader and invisible to somebody using the map. The transferable habit is to read a picture as a document with an author and an hour, exactly as one would read a paragraph.

questions.hint: Ask what the map was made for, and who decided what it should not show.

questions.explanation: A good answer makes the point that a map is a set of decisions about omission, that those decisions are made for a purpose, and that the purpose is dated. The three usual purposes, a military office, a commercial house and a school, each leave out something a modern reader takes for granted, and none of them is lying because the map never claimed to be a photograph. The strongest part of the answer uses a case where the omission is itself a decision, and then notes that such an omission is legible to a later reader and invisible to the person using the map, which is what makes a map one of the best documents in an archive. The transferable habit is to read a picture as a document with an author and an hour, exactly as one would read a paragraph.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Why an official account is read last
questions.learningObjective: explain the place of an official version among the sources of a period
questions.stem: Explain why a period's own official account is usually the last document a historian turns to, and say what it is still good for.

answer.exemplar: The official account is written to be believed, and that is a problem before anybody starts reading it. It is composed by people with a stake in the outcome, at a moment when the argument is still live, and in a genre that rewards a single line of causation, so it will say that a decision produced an outcome and leave out the years in which nothing could be done. It is also the version that will have been repeated, so a reader who meets its claims first meets them without knowing they are claims. That is the case for reading it late. What it is good for is a second thing, and a good answer will name it: it is the place where the state's own account of itself is written down, and a state that is embarrassed by a period tends to describe it in the vocabulary of order and progress, which is evidence about how the state wanted the period seen. Read alongside a wage book, a parish register and a private letter, an official account tells the reader three things at once, which is that the events are broadly as described, that the causes have been arranged, and that somebody considered the arrangement necessary. A historian who skips it has lost the very document in which the state's self-image is most plainly on display.

questions.hint: Ask who the official account is written to convince, and what it is the only source of.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Three questions to ask of any source
questions.learningObjective: select the questions that belong to source criticism
questions.stem: Four questions a reader can ask about a document are offered. Three belong to source criticism. Which three?

options.text: Who wrote it, and for whom was it written?
Why was it written at that moment and not at another?
Which parts are the writer's own words and which are a formula carried over?
Does its phrasing agree with the period the writer claims to be writing in?
options.misconception: confuses a question about a writer's credibility with a question about a document's language

questions.explanation: The three that qualify all ask about the relationship between the document and the person who made it. Who wrote it and for whom gives the writer a position and an audience, and a position in a hierarchy is the first thing a reader needs. Why now asks about the occasion, which is where a report, a request and a justification differ, and a document written at one moment says something that the same writer would not have written at another. The third question is the sharpest of the three, because official documents are built from formulas, and a paragraph that reproduces a formula tells the reader about the office rather than about the event, and has to be set aside before the rest can be used. The fourth is a real question for a historian of language and a poor one for a critic of this document, since what matters is what the writer was in a position to know, not how well the writer could imitate the style of an age.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four is about the writer's position rather than about the style of the text.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: How a record of a period reaches a modern reader
questions.learningObjective: sort routes of transmission into those that preserve and those that lose
questions.stem: A record of a nineteenth-century administrative decision is now read by a researcher. Three of the routes below make the reading possible or reliable. Which three?

options.text: The file is kept in an archive and described in a published finding aid
It is printed in a collection whose preface says who wrote it and when
It is reproduced in a book that gives the archive reference and the date of the copy
It circulates in a version that cannot be consulted outside one building
options.misconception: treats restricted access as though it preserved the record

questions.explanation: A record survives by being findable and by being attributable, and the first three routes supply one or both. A finding aid is what turns a shelf into a collection, since a box nobody has described is a box nobody can find, and a preface that names a writer and a date gives the reader the two facts any source needs before it can be used at all. An archive reference with the date of the copy does something subtler, because it tells a later reader exactly which object was photographed and when, and therefore whether the copy they are holding is the one the editor used. The fourth trap is the one worth dwelling on, since a copy available in a single building is not thereby a lost record: it is a record with a cost attached, and the cost falls on whoever cannot travel. The failure of access is different from the failure of description, and the first is often mistaken for the second.
questions.hint: Ask of each route whether it says where the object is and who is responsible for it.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Captioning a document in an archive
questions.learningObjective: write an archive caption inside a word limit and name what it withholds
questions.stem: Stage one: in no more than thirty words of Spanish, write the catalogue caption for a nineteenth-century administrative file. Stage two: say what a reader still cannot tell from your caption.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: Expediente sobre licencias de apertura de comercios del distrito norte, segundo trimestre de 1887, con solicitudes y denegaciones. Stage two: the caption leaves out who wrote the file, which of the requests were refused and why, what the trade of each applicant was, and how complete the file is, so four things a historian would want are in a box rather than in the caption. A caption is not a summary and the mistake to avoid is writing one. The three parts of the phrase are the three things a catalogue can state safely, the matter, the period and the physical form of the file, and the prepositional phrase con solicitudes y denegaciones names the contents without claiming anything about them. The imperfect of the description would be the right tense if the file were being described from the inside, and the front of the catalogue is normally in the indicative because the record is a thing that is. A better caption would give the reference number as well, which is what makes the item findable, and a worse one would summarise the decisions. The habit worth teaching is to write the caption, then ask which of the six questions a reader arrives with it can now answer.

questions.hint: Ask which of the things a reader needs are facts about the object and which need the file to be opened.

questions.explanation: The two stages are set so that a learner who writes only the caption believes the task is finished, and the second stage is the harder half. A caption is a set of facts about an object rather than a summary of its contents, so the good answer will name the three things a caption can state safely, the matter, the period and the physical form of the file, and then the four it has left inside the box, which is what a historian actually arrives wanting. The grammar point worth drawing out is the tense, since the indicative belongs to a description of the object and the imperfect to a description of the work the file records, and mixing them writes a caption that is about nothing in particular. A better caption gives the reference number as well, which is what makes the item findable, and a worse one summarises the decisions inside it.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Writing a note for a concert programme
questions.learningObjective: write a programme note inside a word limit and name what it withholds
questions.stem: Stage one: for an evening of nineteenth-century music played in private houses rather than in concert halls, write in Spanish, in no more than twenty-five words, the note that introduces it. Stage two: say what your note leaves out about who played and who paid.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: Piezas para salón, escritas para tocar en casas particulares, que se tocaban ante unos pocos invitados y hoy vuelven a una sala con butacas. Stage two: the note leaves out how the pieces were paid for, who the guests were, whether anybody was paid at all, and how a tune for a room of six reached a hall of six hundred, so the economics of the whole evening are outside the paragraph. The grammar is doing real work in the two places it can. Tocaban is the imperfect, since the music played in a given manner rather than at a given moment, and the prepositional phrase ante unos pocos invitados fixes the scale without needing a number. A better note would name one woman who played and one man who printed the music, and a worse one would promise an atmosphere. The habit worth teaching is to ask of any short public text what it has chosen not to make visible, because a programme is written for an audience that has already paid and will not be asked to think about who was paid before them.

questions.hint: Ask how the music was paid for, and whether your note can say so in the words you have left.

questions.explanation: The two stages are arranged so that a fluent note can be produced without noticing what it has left out, and the omission here is a structural one. A programme note for a small domestic evening will say what the music was and how it was played and will say nothing about who was paid, and the reason is a good answer to the second question, since the audience has already bought a ticket and is not being asked to think about the arrangement. The grammar point to draw out is the imperfect, which carries the sense of a manner of playing rather than a single performance, and which is why it is the tense a note uses for a practice. A better note names one player and one printer, and a worse one promises an atmosphere, which is the sentence a programme is written to avoid.
